question: After a consumer notifies a financial institution of an electronic fund transfer error, what investigation and resolution steps are required, and within what time limits?
generated_answer:
## Electronic Fund Transfer Error Investigation and Resolution Requirements

### 1. Qualifying Notice of Error

A financial institution must comply with the applicable error-resolution procedures when it receives oral or written notice from a consumer. The supplied evidence does not establish the precise consumer notice deadline, so no specific 60-day deadline is asserted here.

---

### 2. Standard 10-Business-Day Investigation Period

The default timeline requires the financial institution to:

| Obligation | Deadline |
|---|---|
| Investigate promptly and determine whether error occurred | Within **10 business days** of receiving notice |
| Report results to consumer | Within **3 business days** after completing investigation |
| Correct the error (if found) | Within **1 business day** after determining error occurred |

[C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]

---

### 3. Extended 45-Day Investigation Period

If the institution **cannot complete its investigation within 10 business days**, it may extend to **up to 45 days**, provided it:

1. **Provisionally credits** the consumer's account in the full amount of the alleged error (including interest where applicable) within the 10-business-day period [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]
2. **Advises the consumer within 2 business days** of the provisional crediting [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001]
3. **Gives the consumer full use of the funds** during the investigation [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001]

> **Note on withholding:** If the institution has a reasonable basis for believing an unauthorized EFT occurred and has satisfied the requirements of § 1005.6(a), it may withhold a portion of the provisionally credited amount. [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0002]

#### Exceptions — No Provisional Credit Required:
- The institution requires but does **not receive written confirmation** within 10 business days of an oral notice of error [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001]
- The alleged error involves an account **subject to Regulation T** (margin/securities credit requirements) [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0701_chunk_0001]

---

### 4. Extended 90-Day Period (Special Circumstances)

The investigation period extends to **90 days** (in place of 45 days) when the error involves an EFT that:
- Was **not initiated within a state**
- Resulted from a **point-of-sale debit card transaction**
- Occurred within **30 days after the first deposit** to the account was made

[C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0003]

---

### 5. If No Error (or Different Error) Is Found

If the institution determines no error occurred, or that the error differed from what the consumer described, it must provide a **written explanation** of its findings and note the consumer's right to request the documents relied upon in making the determination. Upon request, the institution shall promptly provide those documents. [C:12CFR1005_1005.11_chunk_0003]

> **Note:** The evidence does not fully establish all obligations that may apply upon a no-error determination (e.g., reversal of provisional credit), as the relevant regulatory text in the available evidence is truncated.

---

### 6. Scope of Required Investigation

A financial institution's review of **its own records** satisfies the investigation requirement (except for transfers covered by § 1005.14) when:
- The alleged error concerns a transfer **to or from a third party**, AND
- There is **no agreement** between the institution and the third party for that type of EFT

judge_corrected_answer:
## EFT Error Investigation and Resolution (12 CFR 1005.11)

**Qualifying notice.** The institution must follow error-resolution procedures for any oral or written notice of error received no later than 60 days after it sends the periodic statement first reflecting the alleged error, provided the notice identifies the consumer's name/account number and indicates why an error is believed to exist (12 CFR 1005.11(b)(1)). The institution may require written confirmation of an oral notice within 10 business days (1005.11(b)(2)).

**Standard 10-business-day period (1005.11(c)(1)).** Investigate promptly and determine whether an error occurred within 10 business days of receiving the notice; report results to the consumer within 3 business days after completing the investigation; and correct any error within 1 business day after determining it occurred.

**45-day extension (1005.11(c)(2)).** If it cannot finish within 10 business days, the institution may take up to 45 days provided it: (i) provisionally credits the account for the alleged error amount (plus interest where applicable) within 10 business days — though it may withhold a MAXIMUM of $50 if it has a reasonable basis to believe an unauthorized EFT occurred and has satisfied § 1005.6(a); (ii) advises the consumer of the provisional credit within 2 business days and gives full use of the funds; (iii) corrects any error within 1 business day of determination; and (iv) reports results within 3 business days of completing the investigation. Provisional credit is NOT required if the institution requires but does not receive written confirmation of an oral notice within 10 business days, or the account is subject to Regulation T.

**Time extensions (1005.11(c)(3)).** 20 business days apply in place of 10 if the notice involves a transfer within 30 days after the first deposit to the account. 90 days apply in place of 45 for completing the investigation if the error involves a transfer that was not initiated within a state, resulted from a point-of-sale debit card transaction, or occurred within 30 days after the first deposit.

**Investigation scope (1005.11(c)(4)).** Except for transfers covered by § 1005.14, review of the institution's own records suffices if the alleged error concerns a transfer to/from a third party and there is no agreement with that third party for the EFT type involved.

**No error / different error (1005.11(d)).** The institution must provide a written explanation of its findings and note the consumer's right to request the documents relied upon (providing copies promptly on request). If it debits a previously provisional credit, it must (1) notify the consumer of the date and amount of the debit, and (2) honor checks/drafts/preauthorized transfers (without overdraft charge) for 5 business days after notification, to the extent it would have paid them had the credit not been debited.

## Liability Limits for Lost or Stolen Access Devices

When an access device is lost or stolen and unauthorized electronic fund transfers occur, the consumer's liability depends on when the consumer notifies the financial institution. The framework is tiered.

### Threshold Conditions (12 CFR 1005.6(a))
A consumer may be held liable only if the financial institution has:
- Provided the disclosures required by § 1005.7(b)(1), (2), and (3);
- Issued an accepted access device; and
- Provided a means to identify the consumer to whom it was issued.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0697_chunk_0001]

### Tier 1 — Notice Within Two Business Days (1005.6(b)(1))
Maximum liability = lesser of $50 OR the total amount of unauthorized transfers occurring before notice.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001]

### Tier 2 — Notice After Two Business Days, Up to 60 Calendar Days (1005.6(b)(2))
Maximum liability = lesser of $500 OR the sum of: (a) $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers in the first two business days, whichever is less; AND (b) the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring after the close of two business days and before notice — provided the institution establishes those transfers would not have occurred had the consumer notified it within the two-day period.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001]

### Tier 3 — Notice More Than 60 Calendar Days After Statement Transmittal (1005.6(b)(3))
- For transfers occurring within the 60-day period: the lesser of $500, OR the sum of (a) the lesser of $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers in the first two business days, AND (b) the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring after two business days.
- For transfers occurring after the 60-day period: unlimited liability until the financial institution is notified — provided the institution establishes those transfers would not have occurred had the consumer notified it within the 60-day period.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001]

If the consumer's delay in notifying was due to extenuating circumstances, the institution must extend the applicable time periods to a reasonable period.

- A financial institution may impose less liability than Regulation E permits, based on state law or the deposit agreement (1005.6(b)(6)).

Initial Disclosures for Electronic Fund Transfer Services (12 CFR 1005.7)

Timing (1005.7(a)): A financial institution must make the required disclosures at the time the consumer contracts for an EFT service or before the first EFT is made involving the consumer's account.

Required content (1005.7(b)), as applicable:
1. Liability of consumer – a summary of the consumer's liability under § 1005.6 or under state/other applicable law or agreement for unauthorized EFTs. Need not be given if the institution imposes no liability, but must be given before imposing any liability (Comment 1005.7(b)(1)-1).
2. Telephone number and address – of the person/office to be notified when the consumer believes an unauthorized EFT has been or may be made (a specific number/address for reporting a lost/stolen access device or possible unauthorized transfer must be provided on or with the statement).
3. Business days – the institution's business days.
4. Types of transfers; limitations – the types of EFTs the consumer may make and any limitations on frequency and dollar amount; details may be withheld where confidentiality is essential to system security (but the existence of limitations must still be disclosed).
5. Fees – any fees imposed for EFTs or for the right to make transfers.
6. Documentation – a summary of the consumer's right to receipts and periodic statements under § 1005.9 and notices regarding preauthorized transfers under § 1005.10(a) and (d).
7. Stop payment – a summary of the right to stop payment of a preauthorized EFT and the procedure to do so under § 1005.10(c).
8. Liability of institution – a summary of the institution's liability under section 910 of the Act for failure to make or stop certain transfers.
9. Confidentiality – the circumstances under which the institution may, in the ordinary course of business, provide account information to third parties.
10. Error resolution – a notice substantially similar to Model Form A-3 (Appendix A) concerning error resolution.
11. ATM fees – a notice that a fee may be imposed by an ATM operator (§ 1005.16(a)) and by any network used to complete the transaction.

Addition of new EFT services (1005.7(c)): If an EFT service is added with terms and conditions different from those in the initial disclosures, new disclosures for that service are required.

Shared systems and service providers: In a shared system, an institution need only make disclosures within its knowledge that apply to its relationship with the consumer for whom it holds an account (12 CFR 1005.4(d)). A person that provides EFT services but does not hold the consumer's account — where it issues an access device and has no agreement with the account-holding institution — must give the § 1005.7 disclosures within the purview of its relationship with the consumer (12 CFR 1005.14).

Periodic Statement Requirements Under Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.9)

General content: Periodic statements must include the same type of information required under 12 CFR 1005.9(b). The full enumeration of required line items is not reproduced in the supplied evidence and cannot be comprehensively stated here.

Exceptions to the periodic statement requirement (12 CFR 1005.9(c)):

### What Constitutes a Billing Error

Under federal regulation, a **billing error** on an open-end credit account includes any of the following reflected on or with a periodic statement [C:12CFR1026_1026.13_chunk_0001]:

6. **Request for clarification** — an extension of credit for which the consumer requests additional clarification, including documentary evidence

## Billing Errors on Open-End Credit Accounts (12 CFR 1026.13)

### What Constitutes a Billing Error [1026.13(a)]
A billing error is any of the following reflected on or with a periodic statement:
1. An extension of credit not made to the consumer or a person with actual, implied, or apparent authority to use the account.
2. An extension of credit not identified in accordance with §§ 1026.7(a)(2)/(b)(2) and 1026.8.
3. A charge for property/services not accepted by the consumer (or designee) or not delivered as agreed.
4. The creditor's failure to credit a payment or other credit properly.
5. A computational or similar accounting error made by the creditor.
6. An extension of credit for which the consumer requests additional clarification, including documentary evidence.
7. The creditor's failure to mail/deliver a periodic statement to the consumer's last known address, if that address was received in writing at least 20 days before the end of the billing cycle.

### What Makes a Billing-Error Notice 'Proper' [1026.13(b)]
A billing-error notice must be a written notice that: (1) is received at the disclosed address no later than 60 days after the creditor transmitted the first periodic statement reflecting the alleged error; (2) enables the creditor to identify the consumer's name and account number; and (3) to the extent possible, states the consumer's belief, the reasons for it, and the type, date, and amount of the error.

### Creditor's Obligations After Receiving a Proper Notice
Time limits [1026.13(c)]: The creditor must mail/deliver written acknowledgment within 30 days of receipt (unless it resolves the matter within that period), and must comply with the resolution procedures of paragraphs (e) or (f) within two complete billing cycles, but no later than 90 days, after receiving the notice.

Rules pending resolution [1026.13(d)]:
- The consumer need not pay, and the creditor may not try to collect, the disputed amount (including related finance/other charges). For automatic payment plans, the issuer must not deduct the disputed amount if the notice is received up to 3 business days before the scheduled payment date.
- No adverse credit reports (directly or indirectly) based on nonpayment of the disputed amount.
- No acceleration of the indebtedness or restricting/closing the account solely because the consumer exercised these rights in good faith; noncompliance may trigger the forfeiture penalty under 15 U.S.C. 1666(e).
- Permitted: collecting any undisputed portion, deducting the disputed amount from the credit limit, and reflecting the disputed amount on the statement if it indicates payment is not required pending compliance.

If the billing error occurred as asserted [1026.13(e)]: Within the (c)(2) time limits, correct the error, credit the account with the disputed amount and related finance/other charges, and mail/deliver a correction notice.

If no error, or a different error, occurred [1026.13(f)]: Within the (c)(2) time limits, mail/deliver an explanation of the reasons the alleged error is incorrect in whole or part; furnish copies of documentary evidence of indebtedness if requested; and if a different error occurred, correct it and credit the account accordingly.

After resolution, if the consumer still owes [1026.13(g)]: Promptly notify the consumer in writing of the amount still owed and when payment is due; allow any disclosed grace period for payment without additional charges; the creditor may report the amount as delinquent only after allowing the disclosed period or 10 days (whichever is longer); and if the consumer re-disputes in writing within the allowed period, the creditor may not report delinquency unless it also promptly reports the dispute, notifies the consumer of recipients of the report, and reports any subsequent resolution.

Reassertion [1026.13(h)]: A creditor that has fully complied has no further responsibilities (other than under (g)(4)) if the consumer reasserts substantially the same error.

Relation to Regulation E [1026.13(i)]: If the credit extension is incident to an electronic fund transfer (e.g., overdraft credit or certain hybrid prepaid-credit card transactions), the creditor must follow Regulation E error-resolution procedures (12 CFR 1005.11, 1005.18(e)) instead of paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (e), (f), and (h).

## Consumer Liability Limits for Unauthorized Credit Card Use

### Core Liability Cap

Under federal regulation, **a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card use shall not exceed the lesser of $50 or the amount obtained by the unauthorized use before notification to the card issuer** [C:12CFR1026_1026.12_chunk_0001].

---

### Definition of "Unauthorized Use"

Unauthorized use means use of a credit card by a person **other than the cardholder** who does not have actual, implied, or apparent authority for such use, **and from which the cardholder receives no benefit** [C:12CFR1026_1026.12_chunk_0001].

---

### Conditions That Must Be Met Before Any Liability Attaches

A cardholder can only be held liable if **all** of the following conditions are satisfied [C:12CFR1026_1026.12_chunk_0001]:

1. The credit card is an **accepted** credit card
2. The card issuer has provided **adequate notice** of the cardholder's maximum potential liability and the means to notify the issuer of loss or theft
3. The notice must state that liability shall not exceed **$50** and describe how to give oral or written notification

---

### Lesser Liability Governs

If the card issuer imposes **lesser liability** than the $50 maximum, that lesser amount controls [C:12CFR1026_1026.12_chunk_0002].

---

### Special Rule for Business Use

If **10 or more credit cards** are issued by one card issuer for use by employees of an organization, the card issuer and organization may agree to liability terms without regard to the standard rules. However, **liability imposed on individual employees** must still comply with the standard limitations above [C:12CFR1026_1026.12_chunk_0002].

---

### Summary Table

| Condition | Maximum Liability |
|---|---|
| Unauthorized use before notification | Lesser of **$50** or amount obtained |
| Card issuer offers lesser protection | **Lesser amount** governs |
| Conditions not met (no accepted card, no notice) | **No liability** |

---

### Note on Electronic Fund Transfers (Debit Cards)

These $50 limits apply specifically to **credit cards** under Regulation Z. judge_corrected_answer: Before the first transaction is made under an open-end credit plan, the creditor must furnish the account-opening disclosures required by § 1026.6 (§ 1026.5(b)(1)(i)). For open-end (not home-secured) plans, the required account-opening disclosures include, to the extent applicable (§ 1026.6(b)(2)): (1) the applicable APR(s), including each periodic rate used to compute finance charges, any introductory rate, and any rate applying after expiration of a premium initial rate (and, where permitted, a range of APRs varying by state or creditworthiness with a reference to where the applicable rate is disclosed); (2) fees for issuance or availability — any annual or other periodic fee (including activity/inactivity fees) with frequency and annualized amount, and any one-time non-periodic fee relating to opening the plan; (3) any fixed finance charge and minimum interest charge (if it exceeds the indexed $1.00 threshold); (4) transaction charges for purchases; (5) the grace period, or a statement that none is provided; (6) where required fees and/or security deposits equal 15% or more of the minimum credit limit, the available credit remaining after those amounts are debited (threshold determined on the minimum credit limit; disclosure based on the actual initial credit limit), together with a statement of the consumer's right to reject the plan and not be obligated to pay those fees until using the account or making a payment after receiving a periodic statement (§ 1026.6(b)(2)(xiii)); (7) a billing error rights reference and the Bureau website reference (§ 1026.6(b)(2)(xiv)-(xv)). Format rules (§ 1026.6(b)(1)(ii)) require specified items to appear in a table, with certain items placed directly below the table and paragraph (b)(3)-(5) disclosures permitted outside the table. Fee collection: a creditor generally may not collect any fee before account-opening disclosures are provided, though membership/application fees may be collected or agreed to beforehand if the consumer may reject the plan after receiving disclosures without obligation (§ 1026.5(b)(1)(iv)). Timing exceptions: charges not required under § 1026.6(b)(2) may be disclosed after account opening but before the consumer agrees/becomes obligated to pay, if disclosed in a manner the consumer would likely notice; and for qualifying telephone purchases, disclosures may be provided as soon as reasonably practicable after the first transaction subject to the stated return/rejection conditions (§ 1026.5(b)(1)(ii)-(iii)). For open-end high-cost mortgages, the creditor must additionally furnish the § 1026.32 disclosures at least three business days prior to account opening, including the prescribed notice, the APR, and the minimum periodic payment example (§ 1026.31(c)(1); § 1026.32(c)).

judge_corrected_answer: Under 12 CFR 1022.43, after receiving a direct dispute notice from a consumer (submitted to a proper address under (c) and containing the required contents under (d)), a furnisher must: (1) conduct a reasonable investigation of the disputed information; (2) review all relevant information provided by the consumer with the dispute notice; (3) complete its investigation and REPORT THE RESULTS TO THE CONSUMER before expiration of the period under FCRA section 611(a)(1) (15 U.S.C. 1681i(a)(1)) within which a consumer reporting agency would be required to complete its action; and (4) if the investigation finds the furnished information was inaccurate, promptly notify each consumer reporting agency to which it provided the inaccurate information and provide any correction necessary to make the information accurate (1022.43(e)). The investigation duty applies when the dispute relates to the consumer's liability for a credit account/debt, the terms of such an account, the consumer's performance/conduct on the account, or any other information bearing on creditworthiness, credit standing, capacity, character, reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living (1022.43(a)). The duty does NOT apply where the dispute relates to identifying information (other than liability), past/present employers, inquiries, information from public records (unless furnished by a furnisher with a relationship to the consumer), fraud/active-duty alerts, or information provided by another furnisher; nor where the furnisher reasonably believes the dispute was submitted by, prepared on behalf of the consumer by, or on a form supplied by a credit repair organization (1022.43(b)). A furnisher is required to investigate only if the dispute is submitted to a proper address under 1022.43(c). The dispute notice must include: (i) sufficient identifying information (e.g., account number and consumer's name, address, telephone number); (ii) the specific information disputed and basis for the dispute; and (iii) all supporting documentation reasonably required to substantiate the dispute (1022.43(d)). A furnisher need not investigate a dispute it reasonably determines is frivolous or irrelevant — i.e., the consumer did not provide sufficient information, the dispute is substantially the same as one already addressed (unless it includes new (d) information not previously provided), or a (b) exception applies. If it so determines, the furnisher must notify the consumer of the determination within five business days by mail (or other authorized means), and the notice must state the reasons and identify any information required to investigate the dispute, which may be a standardized form (1022.43(f)).

## Policies and Procedures for Furnishers Reporting to Consumer Reporting Agencies

### Core Regulatory Requirement

Furnishers must **establish and implement reasonable written policies and procedures** regarding the accuracy and integrity of information they report to consumer reporting agencies. These policies and procedures must be **appropriate to the nature, size, complexity, and scope** of each furnisher's activities. [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]

---

### Three Primary Obligations Under 12 CFR 1022.42

1. **Establish Written Policies and Procedures**
Each furnisher must create and implement reasonable written policies and procedures addressing accuracy and integrity of reported consumer information. [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]

2. **Consider and Incorporate Interagency Guidelines**
Each furnisher must consider the guidelines in **Appendix E** of 12 CFR Part 1022 when developing its policies and procedures, and incorporate those guidelines that are appropriate to their operations. [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]

3. **Periodic Review and Updates**
Each furnisher must **periodically review** its policies and procedures and **update them as necessary** to ensure their continued effectiveness. [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]

---

### Statutory Basis and Rulemaking History

Section 623(e) of the FCRA required the agencies and the FTC to:
- Issue **guidelines** for furnishers regarding accuracy and integrity
- Prescribe **regulations** requiring furnishers to establish reasonable policies and procedures implementing those guidelines
- Issue regulations identifying circumstances requiring furnisher **reinvestigation of direct disputes**

Final rules were published at 74 FR 31484 and took effect **July 1, 2010**. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0632_chunk_0001]

---

### Definitions

The supplied evidence does not contain complete text establishing standalone definitions of "Accuracy" and "Integrity." Those definitions are not reproduced here.

---

### Specific Accuracy Duties Under Section 623(a)

Furnishers must also:
- **Not furnish information** they know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0634_chunk_0001]
- **Promptly notify** CRAs when they determine previously furnished information is incomplete or inaccurate [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0634_chunk_0001]
- **Provide corrections** or any additional information necessary to make the information complete and accurate to the consumer reporting agency [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0634_chunk_0001]

---

### Examination Considerations

Examiners assess whether furnishers have:
1. Established and implemented reasonable written policies and procedures regarding accuracy and integrity [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]
2. Considered the Interagency Guidelines in Appendix E and incorporated those that are appropriate [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]
3. Periodically reviewed and updated their policies and procedures to ensure continued effectiveness [C:12CFR1022_1022.42_chunk_0001]

Examiners also determine whether the entity furnishes consumer information to a consumer reporting agency about an account or other relationship with a consumer, which triggers applicability of 12 CFR 1022.40–1022.43. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0663_chunk_0001]

---

### Consequences of Insufficient Policies

Supervisory experience has demonstrated that **failure to maintain and update** furnishing policies can cause direct consumer harm. For example, an auto furnisher that failed to update its policies to reflect changed vehicle return practices erroneously reported consumers as delinquent for vehicles that had already been returned. [C:sh_issue23_2021-01_page_0019_chunk_0001]

Furnishers are required to establish and implement reasonable written policies and procedures appropriate to the **nature, size, complexity, and scope** of their activities — meaning policies must evolve as business practices change. [C:sh_issue23_2021-01_page_0019_chunk_0001]

### Disputes Excluded from Investigation Requirements

**Credit Repair Organization Exception:**

Furnisher investigation requirements do **not** apply when the furnisher has a **reasonable belief** that the dispute was:
- Submitted by a credit repair organization
- Prepared on behalf of the consumer by a credit repair organization

A furnisher is **not required to investigate** a direct dispute if it has reasonably determined the dispute is frivolous or irrelevant. A dispute qualifies as such under two conditions:

Direct Dispute Exclusions and Frivolous/Irrelevant Dispute Handling

1. Disputes Excluded from Furnisher Investigation Requirements (12 CFR 1022.43(b)):

A. Subject-matter exclusions (1022.43(b)(1)) — the investigation requirement does not apply if the direct dispute relates to:
 (i) the consumer's identifying information (name(s), date of birth, SSN, telephone number(s), or address(es)) — other than a dispute relating to liability for a credit account/debt under (a)(1);
 (ii) the identity of past or present employers;
 (iii) inquiries or requests for a consumer report;
 (iv) information derived from public records (judgments, bankruptcies, liens, other legal matters), unless provided by a furnisher with an account/relationship with the consumer;
 (v) information related to fraud alerts or active-duty alerts; or
 (vi) information provided to a consumer reporting agency by another furnisher.
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0001][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0636_chunk_0001]

B. Credit repair organization exception (1022.43(b)(2)) — requirements do not apply if the furnisher has a reasonable belief that the dispute is submitted by, prepared on behalf of the consumer by, or submitted on a form supplied by, a credit repair organization (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 1679a(3)).
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0002][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0637_chunk_0001]

2. Frivolous or Irrelevant Disputes (12 CFR 1022.43(f)):

A furnisher is not required to investigate a direct dispute it has reasonably determined to be frivolous or irrelevant. A dispute qualifies if:
 (i) the consumer did not provide sufficient information to investigate the disputed information as required by paragraph (d);
 (ii) the dispute is substantially the same as a dispute previously submitted by or on behalf of the consumer (directly or through a CRA) for which the furnisher already satisfied applicable requirements — unless the new dispute includes paragraph (d) information not previously provided; or
 (iii) the furnisher is not required to investigate because one or more exceptions in paragraph (b) applies.
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0003][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0638_chunk_0001]

3. Consequence of a Frivolous/Irrelevant Determination (1022.43(f)(2)-(3)):

Upon making such a determination, the furnisher must notify the consumer of the determination no later than five business days after making it, by mail (or by other authorized means). The notice must state the reasons for the determination and identify any information required to investigate the disputed information, and may consist of a standardized form describing the general nature of such information.
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0003][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0638_chunk_0001]

Supervisory note: CFPB examiners have found that even where investigations are conducted, furnishers must actually review underlying account information, documentation, account history notes, and dispute-related correspondence; inadequate staffing and high daily dispute-resolution requirements have contributed to failures to conduct reasonable investigations.

### 1. Timing Restrictions

A debt collector must not communicate or attempt to communicate with a consumer:

- **At any unusual time**, or at a time the debt collector knows or should know is inconvenient to the consumer

judge_corrected_answer:
Restrictions on the frequency and timing of debt-collector telephone calls (12 CFR 1006.14; timing under 12 CFR 1006.6):

Timing:
- A debt collector must not communicate or attempt to communicate with a consumer at any unusual time, or a time it knows or should know is inconvenient. In the absence of knowledge to the contrary, a time before 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m. local time at the consumer's location is inconvenient. The debt collector also must not contact the consumer at an unusual or inconvenient place (§ 1006.6(b)(1)).

Frequency (§ 1006.14(b)):
- General prohibition: A debt collector must not place calls or engage any person in telephone conversation repeatedly or continuously with intent to annoy, abuse, or harass any person at the called number (§ 1006.14(b)(1)).
- Presumption of compliance: A debt collector is presumed to comply if, as to a particular person and particular debt, it places calls neither (A) more than seven times within seven consecutive days, nor (B) within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with the person about that debt (the conversation date is day one) (§ 1006.14(b)(2)(i)).
- Presumption of violation: A debt collector is presumed to violate (b)(1) if it places calls in excess of either of those frequencies (§ 1006.14(b)(2)(ii)).
- Excluded calls (do not count toward the frequencies): calls placed with the person's prior direct consent within seven days of that consent; calls not connected to the dialed number; and calls to persons described in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)-(vi) (§ 1006.14(b)(3)).
- 'Particular debt' means each debt in collection; for student loans it means all student loan debts serviced under a single account number when obtained by the collector (§ 1006.14(b)(4)).

Related harassment prohibitions tied to calls include not using/threatening violence or criminal means, not using obscene or profane language, not publishing debtor lists (except as permitted), and not placing calls without meaningfully disclosing the caller's identity (§ 1006.14(c)-(g)).

judge_corrected_answer:
Under 12 CFR 1006.6 (Regulation F / FDCPA), a debt collector's communications with a consumer are governed as follows:

1. Definition of 'consumer' (1006.6(a)): Includes the consumer, the consumer's spouse, the consumer's parent (if the consumer is a minor), legal guardian, the executor or administrator of a deceased consumer's estate, and a confirmed successor in interest.

2. Prohibited times (1006.6(b)(1)(i)): No communication at any unusual time, or a time the collector knows or should know is inconvenient. Absent knowledge to the contrary, before 8:00 a.m. and after 9:00 p.m. local time at the consumer's location is deemed inconvenient.

3. Prohibited places (1006.6(b)(1)(ii)): No communication at any unusual place, or a place the collector knows or should know is inconvenient to the consumer.

4. Place of employment (1006.6(b)(3)): No communication at the consumer's place of employment if the collector knows or has reason to know the employer prohibits the consumer from receiving such communication.

5. Attorney representation (1006.6(b)(2)): No communication with the consumer if the collector knows the consumer is represented by an attorney regarding the debt and knows, or can readily ascertain, the attorney's name and address, unless the attorney fails to respond within a reasonable time or consents to direct communication.

6. Exceptions to (b)(1)-(3) (1006.6(b)(4)): These prohibitions do not apply where the collector has the prior consent of the consumer given directly during a non-violating communication, or the express permission of a court of competent jurisdiction.

7. Cease communication (1006.6(c)): If the consumer notifies the collector in writing that they refuse to pay or want communication to cease, the collector must stop further communication about that debt, except to advise that efforts are being terminated; to notify that the collector or creditor may invoke remedies it ordinarily invokes; or, where applicable, that it intends to invoke a specified remedy.

8. Third parties (1006.6(d)): The collector generally must not communicate with persons other than the consumer, the consumer's attorney, a consumer reporting agency (if permitted by law), the creditor, the creditor's attorney, or the collector's attorney, subject to exceptions (e.g., acquiring location information under 1006.10, prior consent, court permission, or as reasonably necessary to effectuate a postjudgment judicial remedy).

## Validation Notice Requirements Under 12 CFR 1006.34

### When Must It Be Sent?

A debt collector must provide validation information to a consumer either:

- **In the initial communication** itself, or
- **Within five days** of the initial communication [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0001]

This may be delivered as a written/electronic validation notice or **orally** during the initial communication [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0001].

> **Exception:** If the consumer pays the debt before the five-day deadline would require the notice to be sent, the debt collector is not required to send it [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0001].

#### 1. Debt Collector Communication Disclosure
The statement required by § 1006.18(e) [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0002].

#### 2. Information About the Debt
The evidence establishes that required debt information includes:
- The **debt collector's name and mailing address** for disputes and original-creditor requests
- The **consumer's name and mailing address** [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0002]

> **Note:** The supplied evidence for additional debt-specific sub-items (such as creditor name on the itemization date and account number on the itemization date) is truncated and does not fully support those details. The evidence is insufficient to confirm those specific sub-items.

- The **end date of the validation period** and notice that the consumer may dispute the debt in writing by that date, triggering the debt collector's obligation to cease collection until verification is provided
- The end date and notice that the consumer may **request the original creditor's name and address** in writing by that date
- A statement that unless the consumer disputes the debt by that date, the **debt collector will assume the debt is valid**
- For consumer financial product/service debts, a statement directing the consumer to additional information regarding consumer protections in debt collection on the Bureau's website [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0003]

> **Note:** The specific URL for the Bureau's website is referenced in the evidence but the chunk is truncated before the URL appears. The evidence is insufficient to confirm the exact URL.

If the notice is sent electronically:
- The debt collector's **website and email address**
- If the validation information is *not* provided electronically, a statement explaining how the consumer can dispute the debt or request original-creditor information electronically [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0006]

#### 5. Spanish-Language Disclosures (Optional but Regulated)
A debt collector *may* include either or both of the following optional disclosures:
- The Spanish statement **"Póngase en contacto con nosotros para solicitar una copia de este formulario en español"**
- The Spanish prompt **"Quiero este formulario en español"** next to a consumer-response prompt [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0006]

If a debt collector includes these optional disclosures and the consumer subsequently requests a Spanish-language notice, the debt collector **must** provide a fully translated Spanish validation notice [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0007].

The validation period begins when the debt collector provides the validation information and ends **30 days after the consumer receives or is assumed to receive it**. The debt collector may assume receipt occurs at least **five days** (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after sending [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0002].

### Form Requirements

All validation information must be **clear and conspicuous** — meaning readily understandable, and in the case of written and electronic disclosures, the location and type size must also be readily noticeable and legible [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0001]. A **safe harbor** is available to debt collectors who use **Model Form B-1** or a substantially similar variation [C:12CFR1006_1006.34_chunk_0005].

Under 12 CFR 1006.34, a debt collector must provide the consumer with validation information either (i) in a validation notice sent in the manner required by §1006.42 in the initial communication or within five days of that initial communication, or (ii) orally in the initial communication. Exception: if the consumer pays the debt before the five-day deadline, no notice need be sent (§1006.34(a)). The validation period runs from the date the information is provided and ends 30 days after the consumer receives or is assumed to receive it; the collector may assume receipt at least five days (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after sending (§1006.34(b)(5)).

Required validation information (§1006.34(c)):
1. Debt collector communication disclosure — the statement required by §1006.18(e) (c)(1).
2. Information about the debt (c)(2): (i) the debt collector's name and the mailing address at which it accepts disputes and original-creditor requests; (ii) the consumer's name and mailing address; (iii) for debt related to a consumer financial product or service, the name of the creditor to whom the debt was owed on the itemization date; (iv) the account number (or truncated version) associated with the debt on the itemization date, if any; (v) the name of the creditor to whom the debt is currently owed; (vi) the itemization date; (vii) the amount of the debt on the itemization date; (viii) an itemization of the current amount reflecting interest, fees, payments, and credits since the itemization date; and (ix) the current amount of the debt.
3. Information about consumer protections (c)(3): the end date of the validation period with statements that (i) a written dispute on or before that date requires the collector to cease collection until it sends verification or a copy of a judgment; (ii) a written request on or before that date for the original creditor's name and address requires the collector to cease collection until it provides that information; (iii) unless the consumer disputes by that date, the collector will assume the debt is valid; and (iv) for consumer financial product/service debt, a statement that additional information on consumer protections in debt collection is available on the Bureau's website at www.cfpb.gov/debt-collection; plus (v) if sent electronically, how the consumer can dispute or request original-creditor information electronically.
4. Consumer-response information (c)(4), segregated and placed at the bottom of the notice under 'How do you want to respond?' and 'Check all that apply:': specified dispute prompts ('I want to dispute the debt because I think:', 'This is not my debt.', 'The amount is wrong.', 'Other...'), the original-creditor information prompt, and mailing addresses for the consumer and debt collector.

Optional disclosures (§1006.34(d)(3)) include telephone contact information, a reference code, payment disclosures, disclosures under applicable law, electronic-communication information (website/email and, if not provided electronically, how to respond electronically), and Spanish-language translation disclosures ('Póngase en contacto con nosotros...' and/or 'Quiero este formulario en español'). If the collector includes a Spanish-language optional disclosure and the consumer then requests a Spanish notice, it must provide a completely and accurately translated Spanish validation notice (§1006.34(e)(2)).

Form (§1006.34(d)): validation information must be clear and conspicuous; using Model Form B-1 (or a substantially similar variation) provides a safe harbor. Special rule (§1006.34(c)(5)): for residential mortgage debt where a Regulation Z periodic statement is required, the collector need not provide the information in (c)(2)(vi)–(viii) if it includes the most recent periodic statement in the same communication and a referring statement on the notice.

question: What account-opening disclosures must a depository institution provide under Regulation DD?
generated_answer:
## Account-Opening Disclosures Under Regulation DD

### Statutory Purpose

Regulation DD (12 CFR Part 1030) implements the Truth in Savings Act (TISA). Its purpose is to enable consumers to make informed decisions about deposit accounts through uniform disclosures. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0746_chunk_0001]

---

### Timing of Account-Opening Disclosures (12 CFR 1030.4(a)(1))

Depository institutions must provide disclosures according to the following timing rules:

| Scenario | Requirement |
|----------|-------------|
| Consumer present at account opening | Disclosures provided **before** account is opened or service provided, whichever is earlier |
| Consumer **not present** at opening | Mail or deliver disclosures **no later than 10 business days** after account is opened or service provided |
| Consumer uses **electronic means** (e.g., website) to open account | Disclosures must be provided **before** the account is opened or service is provided |

[C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0783_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0797_chunk_0001]

---

### Disclosures Upon Request (12 CFR 1030.4(a)(2))

- Institutions must provide **full account disclosures, including complete fee schedules**, to any consumer upon request — whether an existing or prospective customer [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0754_chunk_0001]
- An oral inquiry about rates, yields, or fees does **not** trigger the duty to provide written disclosures [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0754_chunk_0001]
- When written information is requested **in person**, disclosures must be provided **at that time** [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0754_chunk_0001]
- When the request is **not made in person**, disclosures must be mailed or delivered within a reasonable time [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0754_chunk_0001]

---

### Format Requirements for Disclosures

Disclosures must be [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0751_chunk_0001]:

- **In a form the consumer may keep**
- **Clearly identifiable** for different accounts if combined
- **Reflective of the terms** of the legal obligation in the account agreement
- **Available in English** upon request if provided in another language
- **Consistent in terminology** when describing required terms or features

---

### Electronic Disclosures

Regulation DD disclosures **may** be provided electronically, subject to compliance with the **E-Sign Act** (15 U.S.C. § 7001 et seq.). The E-Sign Act permits institutions to satisfy disclosure requirements electronically after obtaining the consumer's affirmative consent. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0751_chunk_0001]

> **Note:** The evidence does not fully enumerate all pre-consent disclosure items required before a consumer may give consent, as the relevant portion of the evidence is truncated.

---

### Coverage Note

Regulation DD applies to all depository institutions **except credit unions** that offer deposit accounts to consumers, including U.S. branches of foreign institutions. Edge Act corporations and agencies of foreign institutions are **not** covered. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0747_chunk_0001]

---

### Accuracy of Advertised Terms

Institutions must ensure that advertised account terms (such as bonuses) are accurate and not misleading. Failure to honor advertised bonus offers to eligible consumers has been found to violate Regulation DD. [C:sh_issue22_2020-09_page_0011_chunk_0001]

Under Regulation DD (12 CFR Part 1030, implementing the Truth in Savings Act), a depository institution (other than credit unions; branches of foreign institutions offering consumer deposit accounts are covered, while Edge Act/agreement corporations and agencies of foreign institutions are not) must provide account disclosures as follows [exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0746_chunk_0001; page_0747_chunk_0001]:

TIMING OF ACCOUNT-OPENING DISCLOSURES (12 CFR 1030.4(a)(1)):
- Disclosures must be provided before an account is opened or a service is provided, whichever is earlier [page_0783_chunk_0001; page_0797_chunk_0001].
- If the consumer is not present at opening (and has not already received disclosures), the institution must mail or deliver them no later than 10 business days after the account is opened or service provided, whichever is earlier (1030.4(a)(1)(i)) [page_0783_chunk_0001].
- If a consumer not present uses electronic means (e.g., a website) to open the account or request a service, disclosures must be provided before the account is opened or service provided (1030.4(a)(1)(ii)) [page_0754_chunk_0001; page_0783_chunk_0001].

DISCLOSURES UPON REQUEST (12 CFR 1030.4(a)(2)):
- Full account disclosures, including complete fee schedules, must be available to any consumer upon request, whether existing or prospective [page_0754_chunk_0001].
- An oral inquiry about rates, yields, or fees does not trigger the duty; a request for written information does [page_0754_chunk_0001].
- In-person requests: provide at that time. Requests not made in person: mail or deliver within a reasonable time (generally no more than 10 days) [page_0754_chunk_0001; page_0797_chunk_0001].

FORMAT (clear and conspicuous, in writing): disclosures must be in a form the consumer may keep; clearly identifiable for different accounts if combined; reflective of the terms of the legal obligation; available in English on request if provided in another language; and consistent in terminology [page_0751_chunk_0001].

ELECTRONIC DELIVERY: disclosures may be provided electronically subject to the E-Sign Act (15 U.S.C. 7001 et seq.). Before obtaining consent, the institution must provide a clear and conspicuous statement of: any right to paper/non-electronic form; the right to withdraw consent and its consequences (including fees); the scope of consent; procedures to withdraw consent and update contact information; and methods to obtain a paper copy and any fee; plus a statement of hardware/software requirements [page_0751_chunk_0001].

NOTE ON CONTENT: The substantive content items that must be disclosed at account opening are governed by 12 CFR 1030.4(b) (e.g., rate/APY information, compounding and crediting, balance-computation method, fees, transaction limitations, and time-account terms). The supplied evidence does not include the chunk enumerating those specific 1030.4(b) content items, so they cannot be detailed here from the available record.

Separately, advertised account terms (such as bonuses) must not be misleading or inaccurate; failure to honor advertised bonuses to eligible consumers has been found to violate Regulation DD (12 CFR 1030.8) [sh_issue22_2020-09_page_0011_chunk_0001].

## Rules Governing Payment of Interest on Interest-Bearing Deposit Accounts

The Truth in Savings Act (TISA) and its implementing regulation, Regulation DD (12 CFR Part 1030), establish the following rules:

---

### 1. Balance Calculation Methods

Institutions must calculate interest based on the **full amount of principal** in an account each day, using either:
- The **daily balance method**, or
- The **average daily balance method**

[C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0789_chunk_0001]

---

### 2. Minimum Balance Requirements

- If an institution requires a minimum balance to earn interest, it **must use the same method** to determine the required minimum balance as it uses to calculate interest [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0765_chunk_0001].
- An institution **may** use an additional method only if it is **unequivocally beneficial** to the consumer [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0765_chunk_0001].
- If the balance drops below the required minimum, the institution **may choose not to pay interest** for those days [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0765_chunk_0001].
- Institutions **must pay interest on the full balance** that meets the minimum — for example, if the minimum is $300 and a consumer deposits $500, interest must be paid on the full $500 [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0765_chunk_0001].

---

### 3. When Interest Begins to Accrue

Interest **must begin to accrue no later than the business day** on which the depository institution receives **provisional credit** for deposited funds. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0766_chunk_0001]

---

### 4. When Interest Stops Accruing

Interest **accrues until the day funds are withdrawn** [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0766_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0804_chunk_0001].

---

### 5. Compounding and Crediting Frequency

- An institution is **not required** to compound or credit interest at any particular frequency.
- However, if it does, it may do so **annually, semi-annually, quarterly, monthly, daily, continuously, or on any other basis** [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0804_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0789_chunk_0001].

---

### 6. Early Account Closure

- If an institution chooses **not to pay accrued interest** when a consumer closes an account **prior to the date accrued interest is credited**, it **must disclose this practice** in the initial account disclosures [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0804_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0789_chunk_0001].

---

### 7. Definition of Interest

For regulatory purposes, **interest** means any payment to a consumer or to an account for the use of funds in an account, calculated by applying a periodic rate to the balance [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0749_chunk_0001]. The available evidence indicates that certain payments are excluded from this definition, but the evidence is truncated and does not fully support enumerating those specific exclusions. No further detail on exclusions can be stated based on the available evidence.

---

### 8. Scope of Coverage

Regulation DD applies to depository institutions (except credit unions) that offer deposit accounts to residents of any state. [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0747_chunk_0001]

Requirements for Calculating Interest on Deposit Accounts (12 CFR 1030.7)

Permissible balance methods (1030.7(a)(1)): An institution must calculate interest on the full amount of principal in the account each day using either (1) the daily balance method — applying the daily periodic rate to the full principal each day; or (2) the average daily balance method — applying a periodic rate to the average daily balance (sum of full principal each day divided by the number of days in the period).

Prohibited methods: The ending-balance method, the low-balance method, and the investable-balance method are prohibited.

Day-count/rate rules: Institutions may apply a daily periodic rate greater than 1/365 of the interest rate (e.g., 1/360) so long as it is applied 365 days per year (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-2). In a leap year, institutions may apply a daily rate of 1/366 or 1/365 of the interest rate for 366 days if the account earns interest for February 29 (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-4).

Time accounts and dormant accounts: Institutions are not required to pay interest after a time account matures (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-5). Institutions must pay interest on funds even if the account could be treated as inactive or dormant (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-6).

Minimum balance consistency (1030.7(a)(2)): For accounts requiring a minimum balance to earn interest, the institution must use the same method to determine the minimum balance as it uses to determine the balance on which interest is calculated; it may use an additional method only if unequivocally beneficial to the consumer.

Compounding/crediting and early closure (1030.7(b)): An institution is not required to compound or credit interest at any particular frequency; if it does, it may do so annually, semi-annually, quarterly, monthly, daily, continuously, or on any other basis. If it chooses not to pay accrued interest when a consumer closes the account before interest is credited, it must disclose this in the initial account disclosures (Staff Commentary 1030.7(b)-3).

Accrual timing (1030.7(c)): Interest must begin to accrue no later than the business day on which the institution receives provisional credit for the funds (consistent with Section 606 of the Expedited Funds Availability Act and Regulation CC Section 229.14), and interest accrues until the day funds are withdrawn.

(Related disclosure of the interest rate and APY under 1030.4(b)(1) and compounding/crediting frequency under 1030.4(b)(2) supplement these calculation requirements.)
